text.p: Governors of U.S. Pacific salmon-fishing states agreed on Wednesday to hold a fall meeting with Canadian officials in an effort to restart long-stalled treaty negotiations on salmon quotas.

The "salmon summit" will include the governors of Alaska, Washington and Oregon and Canadian fisheries officials, but pointedly will exclude British Columbia Premier Glen Clark, whose heated rhetoric has helped raise long-simmering tensions between the two countries over how to allocate Pacific salmon.

The planned summit was announced by Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles after a two-hour meeting with Washington Gov. Gary Locke and Canadian fisheries Minister David Anderson that aimed to reduce the tensions, which boiled over last week as angry Canadian fishermen blockaded an Alaska state ferry for three days in Prince Rupert, B.C.

Anderson reiterated his plans to open a "vigorous" August sockeye salmon season that inevitably will result in a bycatch of U.S.-bound coho, but he pledged to stay in contact with Washington state fisheries managers as the season goes forward.

And he said he would aim to keep the coho catch at what he called a minimal level of 20 to 25 percent of the total, despite Clark's call for a "Canada First" fishing plan in retaliation for this year's huge catch of Canada-bound sockeye by Alaskan fishermen.
Clark and Canadian fishermen contend the Alaskans intentionally overfished, while Alaskan officials say the sockeye bycatch, triple the usual level, was a result of exceptionally strong salmon runs.
The exact date of the summit meeting was not set, but Knowles said Clark would be excluded because only the Canadian federal government has authority over fisheries.
"We want to get the politics out of it," Knowles told reporters after the airport meeting near Seattle. "There is no snub intended or meant."
Knowles also said he had no plans to restore ferry service to Prince Rupert until Alaska receives compensation for damages suffered as a result of the blockade.

Locke and Knowles said they met this week with former Environmental Protection Agency Administrator William Ruckelshaus, appointed by President Bill Clinton as a special U.S. envoy to help resolve the fishing dispute. University of British Columbia President and Chancellor David Strangway will serve as Canada's special envoy.
But officials held out little hope for substantive talks before "stakeholders" from the two sides meet again in the fall.
"We will this year have to manage the fishery without their advice and assistance," Anderson said.
Locke said all three officials at the meeting reiterated their commitment to conserve dwindling salmon stocks.
"No one wins in a salmon war," he said. "What will ultimately happen is that we will all be fighting over two salmon in the Pacific Ocean."

Earlier, Clark said the "Canada First" plan proposes various options to maximize conservation of Canadian salmon "while ensuring Canadians harvest any available surplus that could otherwise be taken by American fishing fleets."

Under one leading scenario, Canadian fishing boats could congregate in southern British Columbia near the boundary between Canadian and U.S. waters and catch salmon that might otherwise head into the nets of U.S. fishermen.
